newsitem.title: JAPAN: Key points of LDP reforms for Japan public bodies.
newsitem.headline: Key points of LDP reforms for Japan public bodies.

text.p: Following are the main points of a reform plan for government-affiliated financial institutions drawn up by a panel of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) and unveiled on Friday.

The proposals come at a time of mounting criticism against public financial bodies, which have been censured for being inefficient and for straying into private-sector business areas beyond their originally stated purposes.
Main points of the plan are as follows:

--The Japan Development Bank (JDB), which makes loans to core industries and domestic infrastructure projects, and the Hokkaido and Tohoku Development Corporation, which offers loans to industries in the Hokkaido and Tohoku regions, will be abolished, and a portion of their current operations will be transferred to a new bank, which will be established in 1999.
The JDB's loans and debt will be transferred to the new bank.
The JDB's assets were worth 15.9 trillion yen and the Hokkaido and Tohoku Development Corporation had assets worth 1.5 trillion yen as of end March 1996.

--Securitisation of the Housing Loan Corporation's (HLC) loans to homeowners, and issuance of bonds by the HLC will be considered, as Japan's financial system reform progresses. The HLC's assets were worth 66.6 trillion yen as of end March 1996.

--The People's Finance Corporation which makes loans to small businesses and had assets worth 9.5 trillion yen as of end March 1996, will be consolidated with the Enviromental Sanitation Business Finance Corporation (ESBFC), which offers loans to businesses such as restaurants, barbers and hotels, in 1999.
The ESBFC had assets worth 1.1 trillion yen as of end March 1996.

--In accordance with a 1995 cabinet decision, the Export-Import Bank of Japan which makes untied loans to developing countries, and had assets worth 9.5 trillion yen as of end March 1996, will be merged with the Overseas Economic Cooperation Fund (OECF), which provides yen-denominated loans to developing countries as a major part of Japan's official development assistance program.
The OECF had assets worth 8.9 trillion yen as of end March 1996.

--The Small Business Credit Insurance Corporation, which encourages lending to small firms by helping protect the lenders against default risk, and which had assets worth 1.5 trillion yen as of end March 1996, will be merged with the Japan Small Business Corporation, (JSBF) which offers loans to small companies, in 1999.
The JSBF had assets worth eight trillion yen as of end March 1996.

--Steps will be taken to make the Shoko Chukin Bank, which makes loans to medium- and small-sized companies, with assets worth 15.9 trillion yen as of end March 1996, more autonomous. The government's stake in the bank, which accounted for 77.8 percent of the bank's capital as of end-March 1996, will be left unchanged.
